newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Curtain drops on Rio carnival parades.
newsitem.headline: Curtain drops on Rio carnival parades.

text.p: The curtain dropped on Rio de Janeiro's famous annual carnival parades early on Tuesday as the last of the top-rank samba schools made a spirited appeal not to let the samba tradition die.

As the sun came up over Rio's 70,000-capacity sambadrome stadium, revellers drifted away to sleep off hangovers or continue on the beach what some call the world's greatest party. Thousands of cleaners took their place to clear up 430 tonnes of confetti, streamers, beer cans and bits of carnival costumes, city officials said.

Every year, the city's samba schools stage four dusk-to-dawn parades in the purpose-built stadium in a bid to become carnival champions, attracting tens of thousands of spectators and millions of television viewers.

This year's carnival brought some 300,000 visitors to Rio, 15 percent more than last year, and the festivities represented a turnover of $1 billion in alcohol sales, restaurant bills and hotel bookings, according to the Brazilian Association of Travel Agents.

As always, the event built up over the weekend to climax on Sunday and Monday night when the top 16 "special group" schools dazzled spectators with towering floats, a sea of extravagant costumes and thousands of samba dancers writhing to the beat of hundreds of drums.

Academicos da Rocinha took the crowds on a magical journey through the world of Walt Disney, while Mangueira made Rio de Janeiro's bid for the 2004 Olympics its theme, and others like Portela and Estacio de Sa paid homage to carnival itself.

Last year's champion, Mocidade Independente, brought the sambadrome to a boil just after midnight on Monday as its 4,000-strong contingent proved it was worthy of the title once again with a magical journey through the human body.

The crowds cheered and waved thousands of white and green Mocidade flags as the dancers and their giant floats depicted the human body from cells and organs to Carnival's more traditional body parts of gyrating hips, bare breasts and G-stringed buttocks.

This year's parades saw the return of the "bicheiros", Brazil's illegal gambling bosses who are largely responsible for bankrolling the four-day extravaganza and who were jailed four years ago on conspiracy and racketeering charges.

They came to watch the parades of the schools they support for the first time after being released from jail last year on a presidential pardon for prisoners on good behaviour and with minor sentences.
